dishes.summary: A dark decoction of roasted coriander seed boiled with ginger and pepper, the household first response to a cold or fever.
Crushed ginger boiled with tea and sweetened with jaggery, reached for at the first sign of a chill or a sore throat.
The sweet water of the orange king coconut drunk straight from the shell at roadside stalls, prized as a cooling remedy in the midday heat.
variants: thambili with the jelly scooped out

dishes.summary: Fresh lime squeezed into iced water with sugar and a pinch of salt, the standard homemade cooler served to visitors at midday.
Strong Ceylon black tea whitened with milk powder and sweetened heavily, drunk at home and at every wayside boutique several times a day.
Unmilked black tea taken with a lump of jaggery bitten between sips, the cheapest and most common household brew in village homes.
Salted dried fish is soaked, then stewed in a coconut milk and chilli gravy that carries a deep salty flavour prized on rainy days and in up-country homes far from the sea.
Dried sprats are simmered in a thin coconut gravy soured with goraka, producing a cheap wet curry that stretches easily across a large family meal.
Fish steaks rubbed with turmeric, chilli and salt are shallow fried until the edges crisp, giving a simple dry accompaniment for rice or bread.
variants: served with a spoonful of lunu miris over it

dishes.summary: Whole herring are simmered in a sharp red gravy that is a mainstay of coastal households because the fish lands cheaply and in quantity.
Northern cooks build this tamarind-sour, deeply red gravy on a distinctive roasted curry powder heavy with fenugreek and chilli, often adding drumstick or brinjal to the pot.
Flakes of hard smoked Maldive fish are pounded with chilli, onion and lime into a dry pungent relish that lifts plain rice, bread or string hoppers.
Thick steaks of skipjack or yellowfin tuna are simmered in a fiery chilli and goraka gravy that forms the everyday centrepiece of a rice-and-curry plate.
Small oily sardinella are cooked whole in a sour goraka gravy until the bones soften, giving one of the cheapest fresh fish curries on the coast.
Pieces of dried fish are fried hard and stirred through onions and chilli into a dry, intensely savoury relish eaten in small amounts alongside a bigger meal.
Small dried sprats are fried until crisp and tossed with onion, chilli and curry leaves to make the cheapest and most frequently cooked protein side in Sri Lankan homes.
Cooked or fried fish is flaked off the bone and tossed in hot oil with onion, chilli and curry leaf until dry, the usual way a household turns yesterday's fish curry into a fresh side.
variants: with green chilli instead of dried
finished with a squeeze of lime

dishes.summary: Canned mackerel or sardines are simmered with onion, tomato and coconut milk into a quick gravy that families rely on when fresh fish is expensive or unavailable.
Fish is poached gently in turmeric-tinted coconut milk with green chilli and fenugreek, giving a mild soupy curry that suits children and elders at the same table.
Meaty yellowfin steaks hold their shape in a dark roasted-spice gravy, making this the fish curry most often chosen when the household wants something substantial.
Cubed beef is slow-simmered with gorakka, roasted curry powder and coconut milk until tender, a staple main in Muslim, Tamil and Christian households and at rice-and-curry shops.
The everyday household chicken curry, in which bone-in pieces are simmered with pounded aromatics, curry powder and coconut milk into a mid-thick reddish gravy served over rice.
Boneless chicken is fried and then tossed hot and fast with onion wedges, capsicum and a sticky chilli-and-soy sauce, eaten as a fiery accompaniment to rice or as a bar bite.
Chicken pieces are marinated in lime, turmeric, pepper and chilli, then shallow or deep fried until the spice crust darkens, giving a crisp dry dish that sits beside rice and curry.
A single egg dropped into hot coconut oil and fried until the white crisps at the edges while the yolk stays soft, eaten with bread, roti or a plate of rice.
variants: served on top of fried rice

dishes.summary: Chickpeas soaked overnight and cooked in a dark roasted-spice coconut gravy, a Muslim household favourite that morning boutiques also sell alongside roti.
variants: with a squeeze of lime and raw onion

dishes.summary: Hard boiled eggs slit and simmered in a spiced coconut gravy, the quick source of protein a household falls back on when there is no fish or meat in the kitchen.
Eggs broken straight into a pan of onions frying with chilli and curry leaves and stirred until they set into soft golden curds, a fast side for bread or rice.
variants: made dry for a lunch packet

dishes.summary: The everyday red lentil curry simmered with coconut milk, onion and curry leaves that turns up at almost every Sri Lankan meal, from bread at breakfast to a full rice plate at noon.
Dried textured soya chunks soaked, squeezed dry and cooked in a spicy tomato and coconut gravy, the cheapest stand-in for meat on a tight household budget.
variants: made with the seasoned packet mix

dishes.summary: Beaten eggs cooked flat with chopped onion, green chilli and curry leaves, a two-minute breakfast that also becomes the filling of an egg roti.
variants: thin omelette shredded into fried rice

dishes.summary: Chickpeas boiled soft and tossed with scraped coconut, salt and a short mustard and curry leaf tempering, eaten at breakfast and carried to the temple on poya days.
variants: sold in paper cones at fairs

dishes.summary: Cooked red lentils finished with a hot tempering of sliced onion, whole dried chilli and curry leaves so the curry turns thicker and smokier than plain parippu.
variants: very dry version for lunch packets
with dried sprats in the tempering

dishes.summary: Shredded godamba roti hammered on a hot plate with chicken, leeks and gravy until everything is chopped into one spicy heap, the country's favourite evening street dinner.
A thick flatbread of flour kneaded with heavily scraped coconut and chilli, griddled dry and eaten hot with a fiery onion sambol.
A hopper with an egg cracked into the batter as it sets, so the yolk cooks soft in the middle of the bowl and is eaten with a spoonful of chilli sambol.
Chopped roti tossed with eggs scrambled straight onto the griddle, the cheapest and most common kottu ordered at a neighbourhood shop.
Day-old rice stir fried hard with egg, spring onion and diced vegetables in the Sri Lankan Chinese style, served with a devilled dish on the side.
A soft wheat dough rested in oil, then flung and stretched paper thin before being folded and griddled, and it is also the sheet that gets chopped up for kottu.
A fermented rice-flour and coconut milk batter swirled in a small bowl-shaped pan to give a lacy crisp rim and a soft spongy centre, made for breakfast or a light dinner.
Rice finished in thick coconut milk until it sets firm enough to press flat and cut into diamonds, made for the first morning of the month and every auspicious occasion.
Roasted rice flour dampened and layered with scraped coconut, then steamed in a bamboo or metal cylinder until it turns out as a crumbly log.
variants: Eaten sweet with coconut milk and kithul treacle instead of curry

dishes.summary: Unpolished red rice takes longer to cook and holds its bite, and many households prefer it as the daily staple for its heavier, more filling texture.
Boiled or rice-cooker white rice is the plate on which almost every Sri Lankan lunch and dinner is built, with the curries spooned around it.
Rice boiled far past done into a loose savoury gruel with coconut milk and garlic, given to anyone unwell and eaten by choice on cold mornings.
Thick slices of bakery bread toasted dark over a flame or in the pan and spread with butter, sugar or seeni sambol for a fast breakfast.
Nests of fine rice-flour noodles squeezed onto woven mats and steamed, counted out by the dozen and eaten with a coconut gravy and sambol.
The meatless version of kottu, built on chopped roti with leeks, cabbage and carrot, and often bulked out with soya meat for a cheap filling dinner.
Red onion and dried chilli crushed on a grinding stone with salt and lime into a fiery wet paste, the standard partner for milk rice and hoppers.
variants: ground on a miris gala stone

dishes.summary: Scraped coconut pounded with chilli, red onion, maldive fish and lime until it turns brick red, the sambol that goes equally well with rice, bread, roti and hoppers.
variants: without maldive fish for a vegetarian version
kalu pol sambol with roasted coconut
kiri pol sambol loosened with coconut milk

dishes.summary: Thin lentil-flour wafers puffed in hot oil until crisp and broken over rice and curry for crunch, a fixture at almsgivings, weddings and Sunday lunches.
Pennywort leaves shredded as finely as thread and tossed with scraped coconut, red onion, lime and green chilli, the raw green that people eat for health on a rice plate.
Sliced onions fried slowly with chilli, tamarind and sugar into a dark sweet-hot relish that keeps for days and ends up inside roti, bread and school lunch packets.
variants: with big onion for a milder result

dishes.summary: A ring-shaped fritter of whipped black gram batter, crisp outside and fluffy inside, central to Tamil breakfasts and temple offerings.
Cassava root peeled and boiled in salted water until floury, broken up by hand and eaten hot with coconut sambol as an afternoon filler.
A fat crumbed roll packed with shredded cabbage and vegetables, despite the name a wholly local bakery invention sold beside fish rolls.
A long ridged sugar-crusted bun named for its crocodile-back scoring, a schoolchild favourite eaten plain with tea.
Coarsely ground soaked dhal shaped into craggy discs with onion and curry leaf and deep fried, sold hot from roadside carts and train platforms.
A soft yeasted bakery bun stuffed with spiced tuna and onion, the single most bought short eat from bread vans and tea kiosks.
Fiery balls of mashed potato and flaked tuna rolled in breadcrumbs and deep fried, sold at every short-eats counter and made in bulk for parties.
A thin crepe wrapped around spiced fish and potato filling, crumbed and fried into the cylindrical roll that defines the Sri Lankan short-eats tray.
Small crimped half-moon pastries holding spiced fish or potato filling, fried until blistered and eaten warm with tea.
A bakery bun filled with dark caramelised onion sambol, sweet and hot at once, bought by the bagful for office tea breaks.
A plain lightly sweetened bakery roll eaten with tea, often split and spread with butter or sambol for a quick breakfast.
Thick set buffalo curd from a clay pot eaten with kithul treacle poured over it, the default dessert after rice and curry across the island.
Peeled green plantain cut into rounds and cooked in coconut milk until starchy and tender, a filling side often chosen when vegetables are dear.
Matchsticks of beetroot stewed in coconut milk until deep magenta and faintly sweet, a favourite for its colour on a rice and curry plate.
Fried brinjal simmered down in a dark, tamarind-edged coconut gravy until it is soft enough to break with a spoon.
variants: white brinjal curry in coconut milk

dishes.summary: Fried brinjal strips steeped in a sweet, sour and mustard-sharp dressing with onion and green chilli, the pickle-like dish that turns a plain rice plate into a celebration.
Finely shredded cabbage wilted for a few minutes with scraped coconut, onion and turmeric, eaten as the dry green element beside rice and curry.
variants: with a scrambled egg stirred through

dishes.summary: Sliced carrot softened in a mild coconut gravy, a sweet and bright-coloured side that up-country households cook almost weekly.
A pale, barely spiced coconut milk gravy sharpened with lime that is poured over milk rice, string hoppers or plain rice to moisten the plate.
Pennywort leaves shredded very fine and warmed only a moment with coconut and onion, valued as much for its cooling reputation as for its taste.
Sliced green beans cooked briefly in spiced coconut milk so they stay crisp, one of the most reliable everyday side dishes on a rice plate.
Finely sliced leeks stir-fried in oil with onion and chilli until glossy and just softened, a dry side that keeps well in a lunch packet.
Long beans snapped into short lengths and cooked quickly in coconut milk, a home-garden staple that costs little and cooks in minutes.
variants: with grated coconut as a mallung

dishes.summary: Tender mukunuwenna leaves chopped fine and tossed briefly with coconut and onion, one of the cheapest and most common greens on a Sri Lankan table.
Cut okra cooked in a spiced coconut gravy, usually fried first so the pods hold their shape rather than turning slippery.
Soft potato cubes simmered in a light turmeric-tinted coconut gravy, the fallback curry almost every household cooks when nothing else is in the kitchen.
variants: thin ala hodi for string hoppers

dishes.summary: Boiled potato wedges tossed in hot oil with onion, curry leaves and chilli until the edges catch and crisp, a dry curry children and lunch packets both favour.
Chunks of pumpkin cooked until they slump into a sweet, mild coconut gravy, a cheap and comforting side that suits both rice and hoppers.
Dried bael flowers steeped into a pale fragrant tea drunk without milk, valued as a calming caffeine-free evening drink.
A herbal porridge built on the strained juice of curry leaves rather than gotukola, drunk in the morning as a remedy for cholesterol and general sluggishness.
A tall pink drink of rose-flavoured milk layered with basil seeds, jelly and ice cream, a Muslim-quarter speciality that peaks during Ramadan.
Finger millet flour whisked into boiling coconut milk to a smooth drinking porridge, taken at dawn with jaggery and regarded as a strengthening breakfast.
A fizzy sweet-hot ginger brew, made at home for Christmas in Burgher families and bought by the bottle to drink with fried short eats.
variants: ginger beer with a squeeze of lime

dishes.summary: A thin green porridge of red rice cooked with coconut milk and the juice of pounded medicinal leaves, drunk early in the morning with a lump of jaggery.
Coffee whipped with milk powder and sugar over crushed ice, a bakery and canteen favourite that outsells hot coffee in the lowlands.
Ripe mango flesh blended with a little sugar, lime and water into a thick cold drink, made at home through the season when the trees drop more fruit than a family can eat.
variants: blended with milk into a shake
left thick and eaten with a spoon
made with papaya when mangoes are done

dishes.summary: Coffee stirred up with milk powder and plenty of sugar, the drink households and boutiques offer in place of tea in the evening or when someone wants something stronger.
variants: with a piece of cinnamon boiled in

dishes.summary: Sour nelli fruit crushed and sweetened into a sharp cordial, drunk for its vitamin content and also sold as salted dried nelli at bus stands.
Passion fruit pulp strained and boiled with sugar into a syrup that is bottled and diluted with cold water, the standard drink offered at home celebrations.
A golden herbal brew from dried ranawara flowers, drunk as a cooling substitute for tea and often recommended for diabetic households.
Roasted semolina cooked into a thin sweet milk porridge, poured warm for children and elders who cannot manage a heavy breakfast.
The tart brown pulp of cracked wood apple whisked with coconut milk and sugar into a thick seasonal drink believed to settle the stomach.
Tiny fresh anchovies are marinated in chilli and turmeric, dusted with rice flour and fried in batches, a northern and eastern side dish eaten bones and all.
Cuttlefish is stewed with heavily dark-roasted spices and sometimes its own ink to give a near-black, intensely aromatic curry served at coastal celebrations.
Whole cracked lagoon or sea crabs are simmered in a thick roasted-spice coconut gravy, a messy and much-loved weekend dish along the coast.
Rings of cuttlefish are cooked slowly in a spiced coconut gravy until tender, a coastal favourite that rewards patience because rushing it toughens the flesh.
Fried fish chunks are tossed at high heat with onion, capsicum and a sweet-hot sauce, a Sri Lankan restaurant style dish that families also cook at home for weekend dinners.
Prawns are seared and finished in a glossy sweet-hot sauce with onion wedges and capsicum, a party and restaurant dish that also appears at family celebrations.
Squid rings are flash cooked with onion, capsicum and chilli sauce so they stay springy, a dish that moved from Sri Lankan Chinese restaurants into home kitchens.
Soaked dried fish is simmered in mild turmeric coconut milk so the salt spreads through the gravy, a soft version often given to children and older family members.
Fried brinjal strips are combined with crisped dried fish and onion so the vegetable soaks up the salty flavour, a way of making a little dried fish feed many.
Drumstick pods are cooked in the fish gravy so they absorb the sour spiced sauce and are sucked clean at the table, a combination found in every region.
The head of a large fish is stewed in a sour tamarind gravy with drumstick and brinjal, a thrifty and much-relished dish especially in northern and eastern kitchens.
A thin, pale coconut milk gravy carrying pieces of fish and green chilli, poured generously over string hoppers or pittu in northern and eastern homes.
Dried sprats are deep fried plain until they shatter between the teeth, eaten as a crunchy side with rice or nibbled on their own.
Battered cuttlefish rings are deep fried and tossed in butter with chilli and onion, a Sri Lankan Chinese restaurant creation now firmly part of local eating out.
Northern crab curry is thickened with roasted rice or coconut and seasoned with the region's fenugreek-heavy powder, giving a clinging gravy eaten with rice using the fingers.
Large lagoon prawns are cooked head-on in a thick roasted-spice gravy so the heads flavour the sauce, a speciality of Negombo, Chilaw and Batticaloa.
Lagoon-caught mullet is cleaned carefully and cooked whole or in thick slices in a coconut curry, common in Negombo, Chilaw and Batticaloa households.
Shell-on prawns are cooked briefly in a spiced coconut gravy so they stay sweet and firm, a favourite when the catch is good or when guests are expected.
Prawns are cooked briefly in mild turmeric coconut milk so their natural sweetness carries the dish, a gentle curry served with string hoppers or hoppers.
Grated coconut is dry-roasted almost to black, ground with spices and used to thicken a rich dark fish gravy that is a special-occasion cousin of the everyday red curry.
Lean sailfish steaks take well to a moderately spiced coconut gravy and are considered a step up from everyday tuna when the household can afford it.
Prized seer fish steaks are treated gently in a fragrant gravy or simply fried, and appear on the table when there is a reason to spend more on fish.
Boneless shark meat is washed well and cooked in a strong sour and peppery gravy that masks its distinctive smell, a long-standing dish in fishing towns.
Firm tuna cubes are cooked almost dry with black gorakka paste, pepper and cinnamon so the sourness preserves the fish for days without refrigeration, a southern coastal speciality.
Tiny dried prawns are crisped in hot oil and tossed with onion and chilli, giving a crunchy salty side that keeps for several days in a jar.
Chips of Maldive fish are fried with onion and chilli until they turn nutty, making a dry accompaniment stronger than sambol and eaten sparingly.
Peeled prawns cooked fast in hot oil with sliced onion, whole dried chilli and curry leaf until the pan is dry, keeping them firm rather than letting them stew in gravy.
Canned fish is broken up and stir-fried dry with onion and green chilli, a five-minute filling for bread, roti or a lunch packet.
Freshwater tilapia from tanks and reservoirs is fried first to firm it up, then finished in a coconut gravy, making it the usual fish curry in inland districts.
Trevally holds together well in gravy and is cooked either as a mild coconut curry or a sour northern-style kulambu depending on the household.
Beef and quartered potatoes are stewed together in a spiced coconut gravy, a stretching dish that feeds a large family from a small piece of meat.
Beef is first cooked down in its spices and then fried in oil until the gravy clings as a dark dry coating, a keeping dish that travels well and lasts a few days without refrigeration.
Beef cooked with dark-roasted coconut and spices until the gravy is thick, near-black and intensely aromatic, a dish reserved for weekends and gatherings because of the long roasting work.
Dark-roasted curry powder and gorakka turn this chicken curry almost black, giving a deep smoky heat that households cook when they want something richer than the everyday version.
Pork is cooked with gorakka and a paste of coconut roasted until nearly black, producing the thick dark southern curry that is the classic dish for family gatherings and toddy sessions.
A thin, pale coconut-milk gravy with a little chicken, turmeric and green chilli, ladled generously over string hoppers or hoppers at breakfast and dinner.
variants: with more chicken as a light curry

dishes.summary: A mild, pale and fragrant chicken curry thickened with ground cashew and coconut, cooked in Muslim households for Ramadan nights, weddings and alongside biryani.
Chicken livers are washed with lime, then cooked quickly with onion, curry leaf and spice into a soft dark curry valued as a cheap iron-rich addition to the rice plate.
Chicken and bones simmered with pepper, ginger and a few chopped vegetables into a light broth, poured for anyone getting over a fever and drunk before a heavy dinner.
variants: made with extra pepper as a remedy

dishes.summary: A gentle white stew of chicken, potato and carrot in lightly spiced coconut milk, cooked for hoppers, bread or as the mild option at a family table.
Pre-cooked chicken is stir-tossed in hot oil with red onion, chilli flakes and curry leaf until dry and glossy, a quick way to turn leftover curry into a fresh dish.
Beef strips are boiled tender, fried dry and then finished with onion, capsicum and a thick chilli-soy glaze, a favourite short eat and rice accompaniment.
Cubes of pork are boiled, fried crisp and tossed with onion, capsicum and a sweet-hot chilli sauce, a bar-and-party dish that has moved firmly into home kitchens.
Sliced sausages are fried and tossed with onion, capsicum and chilli sauce, a fast weeknight dish that Sri Lankan households treat as a full curry rather than a snack.
The northern kitchen's chicken curry, sharpened with the fennel-and-fenugreek heavy Jaffna curry powder, roasted chilli and tamarind for a darker, sourer and hotter gravy than southern versions.
Goat meat cooked northern style with the roasted Jaffna spice blend, tamarind and thick coconut milk, a Sunday and festival curry in Tamil homes across the peninsula and the diaspora.
Beef or goat liver is cubed and cooked briskly with pepper, roasted curry powder and a little sour gorakka so it stays tender rather than turning grainy.
Bone-in goat meat is simmered long with ginger, garlic and whole spices until it falls off the bone, a costlier curry usually kept for weekends, guests and celebrations.
Goat meat is boiled with turmeric then fried down with crushed pepper, onion and curry leaf into a dry peppery dish eaten with rice or as an evening bite.
Fatty pork is boiled in its own spices then fried in the rendered fat until dark and sticky, a dry pungent dish eaten with rice or handed round as a bite with arrack.
The plain everyday pork curry, where several pieces of gorakka cut the fat and give the gravy its characteristic sour edge without any coconut milk.
Chicken simmered in thick coconut milk with green chilli and whole spices but no chilli powder, giving a pale mild curry cooked for children, elders and anyone off strong spice.
Cowpea boiled with a pinch of salt and eaten with scraped coconut and a spoon of treacle, an old-fashioned breakfast that keeps a farmer full until noon.
variants: mixed with grated coconut and chilli

dishes.summary: Raw peanuts simmered in salted water until soft and eaten warm straight from the shell, sold on trains and at beaches and boiled at home when the crop comes in.
Dried cowpea boiled until tender and finished in a mild coconut gravy, a filling and cheap curry in villages where the crop is grown between seasons.
variants: made with the pale mae karal variety

dishes.summary: Boiled eggs halved and tossed in a sticky chilli, onion and tomato sauce mix until every piece is coated, a party plate and a standard on small hotel menus.
Soaked soya chunks squeezed dry, fried until chewy and coated in a sweet-hot sauce with onion and capsicum, eaten with rice or handed round with drinks.
Whole eggs poached in a thin turmeric coconut gravy sharpened with lime, ladled over string hoppers or hoppers so the yolk breaks into the sauce.
variants: eggs beaten in to thicken the gravy

dishes.summary: Whole green gram cooked soft and simmered in coconut milk with turmeric and green chilli, a light curry often made on days when the household avoids meat.
A thin peppery broth of tamarind and tomato boiled with crushed garlic and cumin and finished with a mustard tempering, drunk from the bowl or poured over rice at the end of a Tamil meal.
variants: with more dhal for a thicker broth
extra pepper and cumin when someone has a cold

dishes.summary: A tamarind-sharp lentil stew loaded with drumstick, carrot and onion, made in Tamil households to be poured over thosai, idli or string hoppers.
Green gram steamed until the skins split and served warm with scraped coconut and a trickle of treacle or a piece of jaggery, common at breakfast and for poya-day alms.
variants: with a chilli tempering instead of treacle
cooked with a pinch of salt only

dishes.summary: Boiled chickpeas stir-fried with onion, dried chilli and curry leaves until dry and glossy, served either as a side on the rice plate or as an evening bite.
Kottu made with slow-cooked beef curry and its gravy, ordered late at night from Muslim-run roti shops and heavier than the chicken version.
A richer takeaway kottu in which slices of processed cheese are melted through the chopped roti and meat until the whole plate pulls in strands.

Marinated chicken layered with part-cooked spiced rice and sealed to steam together, the Sri Lankan version milder and moister than its Indian cousin and served with a raita and dark aubergine pickle.
A fermented rice and black gram batter spread thin on a hot griddle until crisp, a staple breakfast in Tamil and Muslim homes and now eaten island wide.
A stretched godamba sheet folded around beaten egg with onion and chilli and griddled until the parcel is set, sold at every roti shop and made at home for tea.
Pittu made with finger millet flour instead of rice flour, giving a darker denser log that is popular with households watching blood sugar.
A dark, earthy flatbread of finger millet flour kneaded with coconut and chilli, eaten by households that want a low-sugar alternative to wheat roti.
Finger millet flour stirred hard into boiling water until it becomes a stiff dark dough, pinched off in lumps and dipped in a strong curry, long a village and estate staple.
Long grain rice fried in ghee with whole spices and fried onion before steaming, cooked in Muslim homes for guests and served with a dark meat curry.
A hopper with kithul or coconut treacle poured into the bowl while it cooks, eaten as a sweet finish to a hopper dinner.
Soft steamed cakes of fermented rice and black gram batter, eaten warm at breakfast in Tamil and Muslim households with chutney and a lentil gravy.
A hopper finished with a spoon of thick sweetened coconut or cow milk poured into the centre so the middle stays creamy rather than spongy.

names.en: Milk rice rolls with sweet coconut filling

dishes.summary: Milk rice pressed flat, spread with a spiced jaggery and coconut pani pol filling and rolled up in banana leaf, cut into rounds for New Year and other celebrations.
The Sri Lankan Malay fried rice, darker and hotter than the Chinese style, fried with a chilli sambal paste and topped with a fried egg.
A layered flatbread of oiled dough coiled and pressed before frying, clapped between the hands to loosen the flakes and eaten with a heavy meat gravy.
The short round samba grain is cooked for guests and special lunches because it stays separate and fluffy, with fine keeri samba reserved for milk rice and festive plates.
Roasted semolina steamed with tempered onion, mustard and curry leaves into a soft savoury mound, a quick breakfast when there is no time for hoppers.
Yesterday's string hoppers crumbled and stir fried with egg, vegetables and gravy, the household way of turning leftovers into a second dinner.
A square parcel of thin roti dough folded around a spiced potato and vegetable filling and griddled, the standard bakery item bought for evening tea.
Leftover rice covered with water and left overnight to sour slightly, then eaten cold in the morning with onion and chilli, a village practice valued for cooling the body.
Rice cooked in coconut milk with turmeric and whole spices until it comes out golden and fragrant, the standard centre of any celebration or party table.
Bitter gourd sliced paper thin, salted or briefly fried, then mixed with onion, lime and chilli so the bitterness stays clean rather than harsh.
Grated raw carrot tossed with scraped coconut, lime, onion and a little chilli, a mild sambol children will eat and a bright filler for a lunch box.
Scraped coconut ground smooth with green chilli, ginger and a knob of tamarind, then finished with a spitting mustard and curry leaf tempering, the usual dip for thosai and idli.
Diced cucumber with red onion, green chilli, lime and salt, thrown together in minutes when the rest of the table is heavy and oily.
Dried fish roasted or fried hard and then crushed with chilli, onion and lime into a pungent relish that a little of goes a long way with plain rice.
Dried sprats fried until they snap and then crushed with onion, chilli and lime, a cheap salty accompaniment that rescues a plain rice meal.
Sliced ambarella, raw mango or nelli tossed with salt, chilli and vinegar until the fruit weeps its own juice, the tart pickle sold at bus stands and made at home in fruit season.
A rough dark paste of roasted dried chilli, maldive fish, onion and lime that is deliberately punishing, taken in small dabs at the edge of the plate.
variants: with a little sugar to round it off

dishes.summary: Limes salted and dried in the sun, then cooked down with chilli and spices until the skins go soft and dark, a sour-hot pickle eaten a sliver at a time.
Half-ripe mango cooked down with sugar, vinegar, chilli, ginger and dates into a thick glossy chutney that is bottled and kept for months.
Thinly sliced red onion rubbed with chilli powder, lime and salt into a sharp raw relish that cuts through oily rice dishes and biriyani.
variants: with big onion rings and vinegar
with a spoon of curd for biriyani

dishes.summary: Carrot, beans, small onions and green chilli scalded briefly and steeped in vinegar with ground mustard and sugar, the sweet-sour pickle that appears whenever guests are fed.
variants: quick fresh achcharu eaten the same day

dishes.summary: Chopped tomato mixed with onion, green chilli, lime and a little scraped coconut, a cooling fresh sambol put together while the rice finishes cooking.
Ripe plantains split lengthwise, dipped in a lightly sweetened flour batter and fried until the coating crisps, the fritter households make when a whole bunch ripens at once.
variants: made with ash plantain and eaten savoury

dishes.summary: Cobs boiled or charcoal-grilled and rubbed with salt, lime and chilli, sold from roadside barrows in the corn season and on hill-country roads.
Sweet potato boiled in its skin and eaten with scraped coconut, a naturally sweet tea-time root that shares the plate with manioc and jackfruit seeds.
The pricier cousin of the fish roll, filled with shredded curried chicken and potato and usually the first item to sell out at bakeries.
Cashews fried in coconut oil and tossed with chilli, salt and curry leaf, the standard bite served with drinks and sold in roadside jars near Puttalam.
A crepe roll built around a boiled egg half set in spiced potato, treated as the more substantial choice on the short-eats tray.
Cassava sliced wafer thin, soaked in turmeric water and deep fried until it snaps, then tossed with salt and chilli, a home and cottage-industry snack sold in clear packets.
variants: made the same way with ash plantain

dishes.summary: Spiralled savoury coils of spiced rice and gram flour pressed through a mould and fried crisp, kept in tins for tea and made in quantity for Deepavali.
A dhal fritter pressed with whole small prawns before frying, famously eaten on Galle Face Green and along the southern coast at sunset.
A crisp triangular pastry of spiced potato or minced meat, a Muslim bakery staple that appears everywhere during Ramadan evenings.
Slices of brinjal, chilli or onion dipped in spiced gram flour batter and fried, sold hot from pavement pans in the late afternoon.
Ripe avocado scooped from the skin and mashed with kithul treacle or sugar into a soft sweet bowl, eaten at tea time in the months when the hill-country trees are bearing.
variants: blended with milk into a shake

dishes.summary: A dense yellow butter sponge baked in a tray and cut into squares, the standard cake for birthdays, tea parties and bakery counters alike.
A steamed or baked egg custard turned out over its own burnt sugar syrup, the dessert that appears at almost every Sri Lankan wedding buffet.
Layers of tea-dipped Marie biscuits set under a chocolate custard and chilled overnight, the dessert almost every Sri Lankan household makes for parties.
Scraped coconut boiled with sugar and tinted pink or green, then cut into squares, a cheap sweet made for school events and almsgiving parcels.
Coconut milk, jaggery and rice flour stirred for hours in a heavy pan until the oil separates and the mass sets into a dark chewy slab.
Thin crepes rolled around a warm filling of coconut cooked down with jaggery and spice, a tea-time sweet many households make in a single pan.
A brittle flower-shaped wafer made by dipping a hot iron mould in rice flour batter and frying it, crunched by the handful at New Year.
Roasted green gram flour bound with treacle, shaped into diamonds and fried in a thin rice flour coat, considered the most laborious New Year sweet.
A steamed custard of eggs, coconut milk and dark jaggery scented with cardamom and clove, brought by Malay households and now the centrepiece dessert of Eid.
Condensed milk and sugar boiled to a fudge and cut into squares while warm, the home-made sweet sold at school fairs and packed into gift boxes.
A batter of rice flour and treacle deep fried in a small pan until it forms a domed cake with a topknot, the sweet that defines the Sinhala and Tamil New Year table.
Coloured sponge layers sandwiched with jam and sliced to show the stripes, a bakery cake bought for children's birthdays and office celebrations.
Roasted rice flour kneaded with treacle syrup, pressed flat and cut into diamonds, one of the easiest sweets on the New Year tray.
Roasted sesame pounded with jaggery and coconut into dense cones wrapped in paper, a Matara speciality sold at bus halts along the southern road.
Scraped coconut cooked down with jaggery or treacle and a stick of cinnamon until dark and sticky, kept in a jar and used to fill pancakes, roti and milk rice rolls.
variants: made with coconut treacle instead of kithul

dishes.summary: A flat chewy fried cake of rice flour and treacle, darker and denser than kavum and shared by Sinhala and Tamil New Year kitchens alike.
Amaranth leaves and their tender stalks cooked down with coconut into a soft mallung, a common cheap green in home gardens and roadside stalls.
Green ambarella cut off the stone and cooked into a sweet-sour coconut curry whose sharpness cuts through a heavy rice plate.
Thick banana peppers cut into rings and fried with onion and tomato into a hot, oily side that is eaten in small spoonfuls.
Finely sliced beans stir-fried dry with onion and chilli so they stay crunchy, the version most often packed into an office lunch box.
Beetroot cut into matchsticks and fried dry with onion and chilli until the edges catch and sweeten, a firmer alternative to the usual coconut milk version and better suited to a lunch packet.
Bitter gourd slices cooked in a thick coconut gravy that softens but never hides the bitterness, often cooked deliberately for people managing blood sugar.
variants: karawila kalu pol with roasted coconut

dishes.summary: Thin rings of bitter gourd salted, squeezed and fried crisp before being tossed with onion and chilli, eaten in small amounts for its bitterness.
Peeled bottle gourd cut into cubes and cooked in coconut milk into a very mild, watery curry often chosen for children and the elderly.
Starchy breadfruit chunks cooked in coconut milk into a substantial curry that villagers treat as a rice substitute during the season.
variants: del kiri in plain coconut milk

dishes.summary: Brinjal strips fried until golden and tossed with onion, tomato and chilli into a dry tempered dish that is faster than making moju.
Large flat butter beans cooked until they turn floury and then simmered in a thick coconut gravy, filling enough that a small pot stands in for a meat curry.
variants: made from tinned beans for speed
cooked dark with roasted curry powder
with a squeeze of lime stirred in at the end

dishes.summary: Shredded cabbage simmered in a thin coconut gravy rather than dried out, giving a soft white curry that stretches to feed a crowd.
Shredded cabbage tossed in hot oil with onion and dried chilli until lightly browned at the edges, drier and sharper than the coconut mallung.
Grated carrot warmed briefly with coconut and onion into a dry, sweet mallung that children eat more readily than most greens.
Soaked raw cashews simmered gently in a pale, fragrant coconut gravy until creamy, a rich dish kept for weddings, almsgivings and guests.
Lengths of drumstick pod stewed in a spiced coconut gravy, eaten by scraping the soft pulp out with the teeth and leaving the fibrous skin.
Sliced cucumber, tomato and onion with shredded lettuce and grated carrot, dressed only with lime, salt and pepper, the raw plate that now sits beside fried rice and devilled dishes at home.
variants: without lettuce when it is out of season

dishes.summary: Firm half-ripe mango simmered with mustard and coconut milk into a sweet, tart curry that appears whenever the tree in the garden is loaded.
Dried green peas soaked overnight and boiled soft before being finished in a mild coconut gravy, a cheap side that households keep in the cupboard for days when fresh vegetables are dear.
variants: cooked dry as a tempering with onion and chilli
with potato added to bulk it out
made with tinned garden peas when time is short

dishes.summary: Peeled jackfruit seeds boiled until floury and then cooked in a spiced coconut gravy, a thrifty dish made from what would otherwise be thrown away.
variants: roasted seeds eaten as a snack

dishes.summary: Leeks sliced into fine rings and cooked with scraped coconut until just soft, a milder alternative to the fried tempered version.
Cassava boiled thoroughly and then simmered in coconut milk, a heavy root dish eaten as a meal in itself as often as it is eaten beside rice.
Several vegetables cut to the same size and simmered together in one pale coconut milk gravy, a Kandyan way of feeding many people from a single pot.
Moringa leaves picked off their tough stalks and cooked quickly with coconut, valued by households as an iron-rich green they can pluck from the garden tree.
Okra fried hard in oil until the stickiness is gone, then tossed with onion and chilli into a dry, crisp side dish.
Pumpkin cooked in a gravy thickened with coconut roasted almost black and ground with spices, giving a dark, smoky curry quite unlike the everyday white version.
Peeled ridge gourd cut into chunks and cooked briefly in coconut milk, collapsing into a soft, watery curry that suits a light evening meal.
Half-mature jackfruit flesh boiled and then finished in coconut milk, filling enough that a village meal in season is often built around it instead of rice.
variants: kos kiri maluwa in white gravy

dishes.summary: Small sesbania leaves stripped from the stalk and stirred with coconut into a slightly bitter mallung that has a long-standing reputation as a health food.
Watery slices of snake gourd cooked down with coconut milk into a soft, gentle curry that suits anyone eating light.
variants: pathola kalu pol with roasted coconut

dishes.summary: Nivithi leaves and stalks stewed in coconut milk into a soupy green curry that is spooned over rice rather than eaten dry.
Nivithi leaves wilted with scraped coconut and onion into a soft green mallung that goes on the plate beside heavier curries.
Sweet potato cooked in mild coconut gravy so its natural sugar balances the chilli, though many households simply boil and eat it with coconut sambol.
Small round wild brinjals halved and cooked in a spiced coconut gravy, faintly bitter and a favourite among older eaters.
Ripe tomatoes cooked down with onion and chilli into a tangy gravy that is spooned over rice, roti or string hoppers.
Diced potato, carrot and beans stewed in a pale gravy of ground cashew, coconut milk and whole spices with no chilli powder, the meatless kurma Muslim households cook to go with rice or roti.
Chopped water spinach stems and leaves flash-fried with garlic, onion and chilli so they stay green and slightly crunchy.
Ridged winged bean pods sliced thin and cooked in coconut milk so they keep a nutty bite, a garden vegetable that costs almost nothing in season.
Cubes of unripe jackfruit boiled soft then cooked long in a dark roasted-spice gravy until they take on a meaty chew, the best-loved of the island's jackfruit dishes.
Black gram and rice ground and boiled into a thick porridge sweetened with jaggery, drunk warm in Tamil homes as a strengthening food, especially for new mothers.
variants: with coconut milk stirred in at the end

dishes.summary: A thin rice porridge flavoured with the polpala herb, drunk mainly as a home remedy for urinary complaints rather than as an ordinary breakfast.
Sarsaparilla root boiled into a sweet earthy cordial served chilled, sold at herbal drink counters as a body-cooling tonic.
Eel from paddy canals and tanks is cleaned of its slime, cut into rounds and cooked in a strong peppery gravy, a rural dish valued as a tonic food.
Roe sacs taken from a large fish are gently curried or fried whole, treated as a delicacy shared out among the family when the fishmonger has them.
A whole fish is scored, rubbed with lime, garlic and chilli and cooked over embers or wrapped in banana leaf, common where a fresh catch is available.
A thick communal seafood and vegetable broth thickened with palmyrah root flour, cooked in a huge pot in Jaffna for family gatherings and shared straight from it.
This small oily inshore fish is cooked whole in a sour red gravy or fried crisp, and appears on market stalls when larger fish prices climb.
Shelled mussels gathered from rocks and lagoons are cooked with roasted spices into a dark peppery curry eaten mostly in coastal villages.
Parati is usually fried or curried simply with goraka and coconut milk, one of the everyday market fish that keeps protein affordable for coastal families.
Fried fish pieces are steeped in a sweet-sour mustard and vinegar dressing with onions and chillies, keeping for days and often made ahead for a rice table.
Green mango pieces are cooked with prawns so their sharpness balances the sweetness of the shellfish, a seasonal northern and eastern combination.
Small prawns are fried and pounded into a dark chilli and onion paste, giving a rich relish that Burgher and coastal families sometimes call prawn blachan.
Fish preserved for months in salt and goraka inside clay pots is cooked into a powerfully salty curry, a southern coastal tradition that predates refrigeration.
Boiled shark meat is shredded fine and stir-fried with grated coconut, onion and chilli until dry and fluffy, a Jaffna dish whose texture gives it its name.
Sri Lankan Malay families thread spiced beef onto sticks, grill it over coals and serve it with a thick chilli-peanut sauce at weddings and family celebrations.
A Burgher pot roast in which a whole piece of beef is simmered slowly in spiced coconut milk and vinegar, then sliced and served in its dark gravy at Christmas and Sunday lunches.
Goat brain is blanched, broken up and cooked gently with onion, turmeric and green chilli into a soft scramble-like curry prized in Muslim and Tamil households.
Cleaned gizzards are simmered until they lose their chew and then finished in a dark peppery gravy, a cheap offal curry that goes quickly in households that like the texture.
Chicken is braised in the sweet water of a king coconut with soft young coconut flesh stirred in, giving a delicately sweet mild curry served on special occasions.
Chicken cooked down with a heavy hand of crushed black pepper and curry leaf until dry, a Tamil-style fry also made at home as a remedy dish during colds.
Liver is cut small, seared hard and tossed with onion, capsicum and chilli sauce so it stays juicy, a standard bite at bars and a quick side at home.
Boneless goat meat is tenderised, fried and coated in the same hot sweet-sour devilled sauce used for chicken and beef, usually cooked when mutton is already in the house.
Duck raised in village home gardens is cut up and cooked long with roasted spices and gorakka into a dark strong curry made mainly in the east and in lagoon villages.
Burgher meatballs of seasoned mince bound with bread and egg, crumbed and fried golden, served beside rice, packed into lamprais or eaten cold at Christmas.
Hare, hunted around dry-zone paddy fields or reared as rabbit, gives a lean gamey meat that is cooked much like wild boar with heavy roasted spice.
Kidney is soaked in lime and turmeric to draw out its smell, then cooked hot and dry with pepper and chilli, an offal dish bought cheap alongside liver at the meat stall.
Minced goat or beef is bound with herbs and spice, rolled into balls and either fried or dropped into a spiced coconut gravy, a Jaffna dish made for guests and festival meals.
Goat meat in a rich pale gravy of cashew, coconut milk and whole spices, the standard companion to biryani at Muslim weddings and Ramadan tables.
Bones and scraps of goat meat are boiled long with pepper and fennel into a thin restorative broth, drunk at iftar, after illness and at late-night eating houses.
Cut ribs are simmered on the bone with gorakka and roasted spice until the meat loosens, then reduced or grilled dry so the sticky gravy clings to each piece.
A mild Burgher-style pork stew with potato and whole spices in coconut milk sharpened with vinegar, cooked as the gentle counterpart to the fiery black pork curry.
A whole bird rubbed with lime, pepper and crushed garlic and roasted slowly over onions and potatoes until the skin browns, the centrepiece of a Burgher or Catholic Christmas table.
variants: jointed and roasted in the pan
finished with a dark pan gravy

dishes.summary: Beef tripe is scrubbed with lime and turmeric, boiled long and then curried with pepper and roasted spices, a chewy well-loved dish in Muslim, Malay and Burgher kitchens.
Cleaned goat or beef trotters are boiled for hours until the gelatine thickens the gravy, a Muslim household dish eaten early in the morning with bread or roti.
Deer meat, once a village dry-zone dish and now rare and legally restricted, is cooked dark and dry with roasted spices or dried in strips before currying.
Lean dark wild boar meat, common in farming villages bordering forest, is tenderised with vinegar or gorakka and cooked into a heavily spiced dry curry.
Split bengal gram cooked slowly with coconut milk and gentle spices into a thick nutty curry, made when the family wants something heartier than red dhal.
Boiled eggs cooked in a gravy built on coconut and whole spices roasted almost black, giving a southern curry with a dark, deeply toasted flavour.
A thick omelette cut into squares and simmered briefly in coconut gravy so it drinks up the spice, a thrifty way of stretching two eggs across a whole family.
Marinated fish steaks are layered with fragrant ghee rice and slow finished on a low flame, a Muslim community dish cooked when fish is preferred over mutton or chicken.
Milk rice cooked with soaked green gram folded through it, making a more substantial set rice for auspicious mornings and alms giving.
A Dutch Burgher parcel in which stock-cooked rice, a mixed meat curry, aubergine pickle, fried meatballs and a shrimp paste sambol are wrapped in banana leaf and baked together.
Goat meat braised until it falls off the bone and layered with spiced rice for weddings and the big feast days of the Muslim calendar.
Pittu steamed from dried palmyra tuber flour, a Jaffna and Vanni staple with a dark colour and a faintly bitter sweetness unlike the rice version.
A thick rice porridge cooked with meat, vegetables and gentle spices, prepared in mosque kitchens and Muslim homes to break the fast at sunset during Ramadan.
Rice and split green gram boiled together to a soft mash and seasoned with crushed pepper, cumin and ginger fried in ghee, the savoury breakfast counterpart to the sweet Pongal.
variants: with extra pepper for cold mornings

dishes.summary: A thick fermented rice batter sweetened with jaggery and steamed in small cups into a soft spongy cake, made for tea and for temple offerings.
Rice and split green gram boiled in milk until it overflows the pot, then sweetened with jaggery and ghee, cooked by Tamil households to mark the Thai Pongal harvest festival.
Raw beetroot grated fine and mixed with coconut, lime, onion and chilli into a sweet-earthy sambol that stains the whole plate pink.
The small fierce kochchi chillies from the home garden crushed with onion, lime and salt into a relish so hot that a teaspoon serves four people.
Curd whisked loose and mixed with chopped cucumber, onion and green chilli, served cold beside biriyani to take the edge off its heat.
Dates simmered with tamarind, chilli and a little sugar into a dark sticky chutney that is put out with rice and short eats during Ramadan.
A long-keeping pickle of fried vegetables, dates and cashew in a thick mustard, vinegar and chilli dressing, made in Malay and Muslim households at festival time and given away in jars.
Mint ground with green chilli, onion, ginger and lime into a fresh green paste, spooned beside biriyani and fried rice to lift the heaviness.
Limes packed in coarse salt and left in the sun for months until they turn soft and brown, then eaten in slivers with rice or stirred into gravies for sourness.
Tomatoes cooked down with onion, dried chilli and a mustard tempering into a soft tangy chutney eaten with thosai, pittu or a slice of bread.
Jackfruit seeds saved from the fruit, boiled in salted water and peeled by hand, a free seasonal snack in villages with a jak tree.
Cubes of ash pumpkin soaked in lime water and candied in heavy syrup until translucent, kept in jars and used in rich cake as well as eaten alone.
The near-black southern version of dodol, cooked far longer with more jaggery and cashew until it glistens with oil, closely associated with Hambantota.
Coiled rings of black gram batter fried and then soaked in warm treacle syrup, an old New Year sweet less common than kavum today.
A Portuguese-descended Burgher layer cake built by grilling one thin spiced batter layer at a time until a striped tower forms, made only for big occasions.
Stale bread soaked in sweetened egg custard and baked with a caramel base, a thrifty Burgher dessert that turns up at Christmas and family lunches.
A buttery yeasted Dutch-origin cake baked in a fluted mould and eaten in slices with butter and Edam cheese on Christmas morning.
A dark moist cake of scraped coconut and jaggery heavy with spice and preserved fruit, baked for Christmas in Burgher and coastal Catholic homes.
A fragile fried lattice of rice flour batter drizzled with coloured treacle threads, a showpiece sweet now made mainly by older cooks in the south.
A fudgy semolina and cashew cake perfumed with rose water and spice, a Portuguese-descended Burgher recipe baked for Christmas and weddings.
A glossy translucent sweet of cornflour cooked with sugar and ghee until it turns chewy, studded with cashew and cut into blocks for Eid and weddings.
Firm balls of roasted rice flour bound with treacle and a hint of pepper, an old village sweet that keeps for weeks and is loved by children.
A grainy set pudding of rice flour, coconut milk and jaggery studded with cashew, traditionally cut into squares for Kandyan festive tables.
A dark boozy fruit and cashew cake wrapped in paper to mature, cut into small squares and given to neighbours through the Christmas season.
A sweetened finger millet dough folded inside a kenda leaf and steamed, giving a smoky-edged parcel eaten by hand in the hill country.

names.en: String hopper rolls with coconut filling

dishes.summary: String hopper dough squeezed over a sweet coconut and treacle filling and steamed into a stuffed roll, eaten warm at breakfast or tea.
Spiral fritters piped straight into hot oil and drenched in kithul syrup so they stay sticky, sold in cellophane packets around the New Year.
Fine vermicelli browned in ghee and then boiled down in sweetened milk with cardamom, cashew and sultanas, ladled out warm at the end of a festival meal.
variants: made with jaggery instead of sugar
with coconut milk in place of cow milk

dishes.summary: Cubes of white ash pumpkin cooked in a pale coconut gravy into a very mild, watery curry often given to people recovering from illness.
Chopped banana blossom cooked in a spiced coconut gravy until dark and tender, heavier and more filling than the dry mallung version.
Banana blossom florets cleaned of their stiff parts, chopped very fine and cooked with coconut, a patient dish usually made when the garden yields a flower.
The tender inner core of the plantain stem sliced across, soaked to keep it pale and then cooked lightly with coconut, a dish Tamil households cook for its digestive reputation.
Cauliflower florets cooked in a light spiced gravy or fried dry with onion, a newer vegetable that has settled comfortably into the Sri Lankan rice plate.
Thick-skinned local cucumber cut into pieces and cooked briefly in coconut milk, a cooling curry usually made when the crop is cheap and plentiful.
Striped wild brinjals halved and cooked in a dark sour gravy, a village curry with a distinct bitterness that older generations look for.
Whole peeled garlic cloves stewed slowly in coconut milk until sweet and soft, a pungent side dish also cooked as a remedy for coughs and colds.
Peeled habarala stems cooked long with goraka or tamarind to remove the itch before being finished in a spiced coconut gravy, a rural dish that demands careful preparation.
The needle-fine leaves of the wild asparagus creeper stripped from thorny stems and cooked with coconut, a herbal mallung eaten mainly for its traditional tonic reputation.
Small innala tubers scrubbed, boiled and then fried with onion and chilli, a crunchy dry dish that also turns up boiled and salted as a tea-time snack.
Boiled jackfruit flesh shredded by hand and tossed dry with coconut, onion and pepper, a filling mallung that turns leftover kos into a fresh dish.
Dry-zone kekiri melon cut up and cooked in coconut milk into a soft, cooling curry that appears mainly during the harvest months.
variants: ripe kekiri eaten raw with sugar

dishes.summary: Chunks of kiri ala yam boiled well and finished in coconut milk, a starchy village curry cooked mostly when the yam is dug up from the home garden.
Sliced kohila rhizome boiled well and then cooked in a dark spiced gravy, a marshland vegetable with a firm bite that is prized in village cooking.
The young shoots and leaves of the kohila plant chopped fine and cooked with coconut, a rural mallung that must be cooked properly to lose its itch.
Peeled kohlrabi bulbs cut into cubes and cooked in coconut gravy, a hill-country vegetable that turns sweet and firm rather than watery.
variants: with the leaves cooked as mallung

dishes.summary: Rings of lotus rhizome from a tank or paddy pond boiled long and finished in a spiced coconut gravy, a dish associated with temple almsgivings and Poya meals.
Oyster mushrooms torn into strips and cooked in a spiced coconut gravy, treated by many vegetarian households as their meat substitute of choice.
Small red onions cooked whole in a dark sour gravy until jammy and sweet, a strongly flavoured side eaten in small amounts with rice or string hoppers.
variants: lunu miris style with maldive fish

dishes.summary: Pineapple wedges cooked with mustard, chilli and coconut milk into a sweet-hot curry usually served when there are guests at the table.
White radish sliced and simmered in coconut milk until its sharpness mellows, a cheap up-country curry that is also cooked when someone has a cold.
Creeping sarana leaves gathered from waste ground and cooked with coconut into a mallung eaten as much for its traditional medicinal value as for the meal.
Young jackfruit cooked down with plenty of goraka and pepper into a dark, sour, almost dry curry made in the southern style of ambul thiyal.
variants: with coconut milk added at the end
black polos with roasted coconut paste

dishes.summary: Small spiny gourds sliced and cooked in a spiced coconut gravy, milder than ordinary bitter gourd and gathered mostly from village fences in the rainy months.
Taro corms peeled, boiled with a little sourness to take away the itch and then cooked in a spiced coconut gravy into a dense root curry.
variants: with the young leaves as mallung

dishes.summary: Small wild brinjals fried whole and steeped in a sweet-sour mustard dressing, keeping for days and often packed for journeys and picnics.
Small bitter turkey berries crushed and cooked in a spiced coconut gravy, eaten sparingly and often described as a tonic rather than a treat.
Winged beans chopped very fine across the ridges and cooked briefly with coconut into a crunchy dry mallung.
variants: raw as a salad with lime
